steps.user_message: I'm preparing my 2024 taxes and could use your help. Situation: married filing jointly, Phoenix AZ. W-2 from Metro Consulting: $82,350. Side income: $14,600 from web design (3 clients). Interest $1,780 (Synchrony Bank), dividends $550 (Robinhood). Home office: 110 sq ft, rent $1,600/month, apartment 780 sq ft. Deductions: student loan interest $4,250 (Sallie Mae, 2019–2020); charity $1,100 to Local United Way have the receipt; unreimbursed expenses $950. Can you help me figure out deductions, standard vs itemized, and home office treatment—and which forms to use?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — this is enough to get a clear picture. I’ll summarize which deductions you can take, whether you should itemize, how to treat the home office, which forms you’ll use, and give estimated numbers so you can see the tax impact. I’ll also list a few follow-up questions so I can refine numbers if you want.

Quick summary (bottom-line)
- Likely take the 2024 standard deduction for Married Filing Jointly: $29,200 — this will be larger than your likely itemized deductions (you only listed $1,100 in cash charity).
- Home-office deduction is available for your web‑design self‑employment income (Schedule C). You can claim it whether or not you itemize.
- Student‑loan interest: you appear eligible for the student loan interest adjustment, but the deduction is limited to $2,500 (even though you paid $4,250). Based on the income you gave, you should qualify for the full $2,500 (see caveat below).
- You will have self‑employment tax on the web‑design income and can deduct one‑half of that as an adjustment to income.
- Forms you’ll generally use: Form 1040, Schedule 1, Schedule C, Schedule SE, Form 8829 (if you use actual home‑office method), and Form 8995 (QBI 20% deduction — simplified) if you claim the qualified business income deduction. Schedule A only if you choose to itemize (doesn’t look useful here).

Inputs I used (from your note)
- Filing status: Married filing jointly, Phoenix AZ
- W‑2 (Metro Consulting): $82,350
- Self‑employment/web design income: $14,600 (3 clients)
- Interest (Synchrony): $1,780
- Dividends (Robinhood): $550
- Rent: $1,600/month => $19,200/year; apartment size 780 sq ft; home office 110 sq ft
- Charity: $1,100 (receipt)
- Student loan interest: $4,250 (you said Sallie Mae; I assume this was paid in the tax year you’re preparing)
- “Unreimbursed expenses” $950 — I need to know whether these are business expenses (for the web design) or employee expenses for the W‑2 job.

Key rules that apply
- Standard vs itemized: Itemized deductions include charitable gifts, state/local taxes (SALT cap $10k), mortgage interest, medical above 7.5% of AGI, etc. Unreimbursed employee expenses are NOT deductible for W‑2 employees for tax years 2018–2025 under TCJA. With only $1,100 charitable contributions listed your itemized total will be far below the MFJ 2024 standard deduction ($29,200).
- Student loan interest deduction: up to $2,500, an adjustment to income (reported on Schedule 1). There are income phaseouts; with your income levels you appear to be under the phaseout (so you should get the full $2,500), but I’ll flag that if your MAGI is different (e.g., spouse’s income or other adjustments) it could reduce or eliminate the deduction.
- Self‑employment tax: You pay SE tax (Social Security + Medicare) on net self‑employment profit. You may deduct one‑half of SE tax as an adjustment to income (Schedule 1).
- Home office: Allowed for self‑employed Schedule C filers only (not for W‑2 employment). Two methods:
  - Simplified: $5 per sq ft up to 300 sq ft = 110 sq ft * $5 = $550.
  - Actual: allocate actual home expenses to the business by % of space. Your % = 110/780 = 14.1026%. For rent only that portion = 14.1026% * $19,200 = $2,707.69. (You can also allocate utilities, renter’s insurance, repairs, etc., if documented.) If you use the actual method you’ll complete Form 8829 and transfer the allowable amount to Schedule C. The actual method here gives a much larger deduction than the simplified method based on rent alone.

Estimated calculations (rounded) — shows impact of home-office method and whether the $950 is a business expense
Base total income = 82,350 + 14,600 + 1,780 + 550 = $99,280.

Scenario A — Actual home office (rent portion $2,707.69), assume no other business expenses:
- Net Schedule C profit = 14,600 − 2,707.69 = 11,892.31
- Self‑employment tax ≈ $1,679 (Schedule SE)
- Half SE deduction (adjustment to income) ≈ $840
- Student loan interest deduction = $2,500 (max, assuming you’re under the phaseout)
- AGI ≈ 99,280 − 840 − 2,500 = ≈ $95,940
- Standard deduction (MFJ) = $29,200 ⇒ taxable income before QBI ≈ $66,740
- QBI (20% of qualified business income): 20% × $11,892 ≈ $2,378 (Form 8995) — reduces taxable income further ⇒ taxable ≈ $64,362
- Self‑employment tax still owed ≈ $1,679 (paid separately; half already deducted above)

Scenario B — Simplified home office ($550):
- Net Schedule C profit = 14,600 − 550 = 14,050
- SE tax ≈ $1,987; half SE ≈ $993
- AGI ≈ 99,280 − 993 − 2,500 = ≈ $95,787
- Taxable before QBI ≈ $66,587
- QBI ≈ 20% × 14,050 = $2,810 ⇒ taxable ≈ $63,777
- SE tax ≈ $1,987

Scenario C — Actual home office + $950 is a business expense (i.e., your “unreimbursed expenses” are business expenses, not employee expenses):
- Business expenses = $2,707.69 + $950 = $3,657.69
- Net Schedule C profit = 14,600 − 3,657.69 = 10,942.31
- SE tax ≈ $1,545; half SE ≈ $773
- AGI ≈ 99,280 − 773 − 2,500 = ≈ $96,007
- Taxable before QBI ≈ $66,807
- QBI ≈ 20% × 10,942 ≈ $2,188 ⇒ taxable ≈ $64,619
- SE tax ≈ $1,545

Notes about the numbers
- These are estimates to illustrate the relative effects (rounded). I did not compute your final federal income tax liability (tax brackets, credits), but these show how the home office and business expenses lower taxable income and SE tax.
- The actual method of computing the home office includes more than rent (utilities, renter’s insurance, repairs). If you have those records, actual method will likely be even more beneficial.
- The home-office deduction reduces your Schedule C net profit (and therefore also reduces SE tax). You can claim the home office even though you take the standard deduction on Form 1040.
- Student loan interest deduction is capped at $2,500 and is an above‑the‑line deduction on Schedule 1; you must have actually paid the interest during the tax year and meet the income rules.
- You should also check for 1099‑NEC / 1099‑K from your clients, Form 1099‑INT (interest) and 1099‑DIV (dividends); include those amounts on the return.

Which IRS forms to use
- Form 1040 — main return.
- Schedule 1 (Form 1040) — report adjustments to income (student loan interest deduction, one‑half of SE tax is reported here).
- Schedule C (Form 1040) — report the web‑design business income and expenses.
- Schedule SE — compute self‑employment tax.
- Form 8829 — if you use the actual method for business use of your home (calculate allowable portion of rent, utilities, etc.). If you use the simplified method, you do NOT file Form 8829; instead report the simplified deduction on Schedule C.
- Form 8995 — simplified QBI deduction (20% of qualified business income). Your combined taxable income is far below the phaseout thresholds, so the simplified Form 8995 should apply.
- Schedule A (Form 1040) — only if you elect to itemize (not recommended here unless you have significantly more itemizable deductions).
- State return: Arizona resident return (AZ Form 140 or current Arizona form) — state rules differ; Arizona starts with federal AGI but check state-specific adjustments.

Practical steps / documents to gather
- W‑2 from Metro Consulting
- 1099‑NEC/1099‑K or records showing the $14,600 self‑employment receipts
- 1099‑INT from Synchrony, 1099‑DIV from Robinhood
- Student loan interest statement (1098‑E or lender statement showing interest paid)
- Receipts for charitable donations (you already have the receipt)
- Documentation of home office (floorplan/photos), rent receipts, utility bills, renter’s insurance, any expenses you plan to allocate
- Records for the $950 — clarify whether these are business expenses (keep receipts/invoices)
- Any estimated tax payments you made in the year

Questions for you (so I can refine the numbers)
1. Are the $950 “unreimbursed expenses” related to the web‑design business (supplies, software, vendor fees, travel, etc.)? If yes, they are business expenses and should be on Schedule C; if they are unreimbursed employee expenses for the W‑2 job, they are NOT deductible.
2. Was the $4,250 student loan interest actually paid during the tax year you’re preparing (i.e., paid in 2024)? Is the loan in your name (or jointly), and did your spouse also pay interest?
3. Do you have utility bills, renter’s insurance, repairs, or other housing-related expenses you want to allocate to the home office (these increase the actual-method deduction)?
4. Did you receive 1099‑NEC or 1099‑K for the web‑design income? Any retirement contributions (IRA, 401(k), SEP IRA) or other above‑the‑line deductions?
5. Do you want me to prepare a tighter numeric worksheet (with final AGI, SE tax, estimated federal income tax) and a checklist of the exact lines/forms to fill out?

If you want, I can:
- Prepare a tighter worksheet that produces estimated federal tax due/refund using the actual tax brackets and your precise inputs.
- Draft the text / checklist you can use when filling Schedule C, Form 8829 (if we pick actual method), Schedule SE, and Form 8995.
- Walk you through how to fill Form 8829 (rows you’ll use) or show how to record simplified method on Schedule C.

Which next step would you like?
